title: Latino Voters Swing Back Toward Democrats Amid Frustration Over Economy and Aggressive Deportations, New Poll Shows
snippet: A dramatic shift in Hispanic voter sentiment could threaten Republican congressional majorities ahead of the 2026 midterms, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo survey.
content:
WASHINGTON — Two years after aiding Donald Trump's return to the White House, Latino voters appear to be turning away from the president and the Republican Party in startling numbers, driven by persistent anxieties over the cost of living and deep unease with federal deportation tactics.

A fresh NBC News/Telemundo poll released this week reveals a sharp drop in support for Trump among Hispanic voters, offering Democrats a crucial opening ahead of midterm elections that could hinge on heavily Latino battlegrounds across Texas, Florida, Nevada, and beyond.

A Dramatic Reversal from 2024 Trends

According to the survey, Trump's approval rating among Latino voters has plummeted to 27%. A vast majority — roughly three in four — express strong dissatisfaction with his handling of the economy and rising living expenses, while two-thirds believe his administration's deportation enforcement measures have gone too far.

The shifting ground has reshaped the national political landscape. Hispanic voters currently favor Democratic control of Congress by a 24-point margin (59% to 35%), doubling the advantage Democrats held with the demographic at this point in 2024. On the vital question of economic stewardship, Democrats now hold a 21-point lead among Latinos — a massive turnaround from 2024, when Trump led on the issue by 4 percentage points.

"What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier," said Republican pollster Micah Roberts of Public Opinion Strategies, who co-conducted the survey with Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates. Roberts characterized the post-2024 shift among Hispanic voters — whom he described as "the swingiest of swing groups" — as "stunning."

Economic Strain and Aggressive Immigration Tactics Drive Voter Backlash

Inflation remains the primary catalyst behind the voter dissatisfaction. Over 60% of Hispanic respondents report that their household income is failing to keep pace with inflation, with 65% stating that administration policies have actively harmed economic conditions.

Voter buyer's remorse is already surfacing among former Trump supporters. Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who backed Trump in 2024 after years of voting Democratic, described feeling deep regret over her choice.

"It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake," Santiago said, criticizing the president's deportation measures as "brutal" and lamenting ongoing financial pressures on her family.

While 83% of surveyed Latinos support deporting undocumented immigrants convicted of violent crimes, only 37% endorse sweeping, indiscriminate deportations. Nearly a third of respondents reported that they or someone close to them have begun carrying identification documents out of fear of ICE enforcement encounters.

Warning Signs for Both Parties Ahead of 2026

The changing dynamics could destabilize congressional maps in Texas and Florida, where Republicans drew heavily Hispanic districts expecting lasting realignment. Analysts note that 54% of Latino voters explicitly intend to use their midterm ballot to voice opposition to the Trump administration.

However, the survey offers cautionary notes for Democrats as well. Despite the GOP's declining favorability, the Democratic Party's overall image among Latino voters has not significantly improved, with 42% holding a negative view.

"Any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats," Cardona-Arroyo cautioned, raising questions about whether the strategy will remain viable beyond the midterms.

The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters between Sept. 21 and Sept. 28, carrying a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.
